passages.text: The role of group III/IV afferent feedback in the ventilatory, pressor and metabolic responses to exercise in normoxia and hypoxia

Group III/IV muscle afferents play a prominent role in ensuring appropriate arterial oxygenation during exercise. <sentence_start/>Exercise in hypoxia poses a major cardiorespiratory challenge due to reduced inspired oxygen pressure (P<sub>I</sub>O<sub>2</sub>). <sentence_start/>Although humans adapt powerfully to hypoxia, the contribution of group III/IV afferents to ventilatory, pressor and metabolic responses to exercise in chronic hypoxia remains unknown. <sentence_start/>Fourteen healthy participants completed cycling trials with (placebo) and without (25 μg intrathecal fentanyl) intact group III/IV afferent feedback in three settings: (1) normoxia, P<sub>I</sub>O<sub>2</sub> = 139 mmHg; (2) acute hypoxia, P<sub>I</sub>O<sub>2</sub> = 90 mmHg; and (3) chronic hypoxia, after 7-9 days of acclimatisation to 3800 m, P<sub>I</sub>O<sub>2</sub> = 90 mmHg. <sentence_start/>Participants completed three 3-min stages at matched absolute intensities corresponding to 45%, 60% and 75% sea-level maximal aerobic power. <sentence_start/>Ventilation, pulmonary gas exchange, arterial blood gases and blood pressure were measured. <sentence_start/>Fentanyl suppressed exercise hyperpnoea similarly across environments (<italic>P</italic> < 0.001) but produced larger reductions in arterial oxygenation in hypoxia, lowering saturation by ~3%-5% and content by ~0.7-1.0 ml dL<sup>−1</sup> (<italic>condition</italic>×<italic>P</italic><italic><sub>I</sub></italic><italic>O</italic><italic><sub>2</sub></italic>, <italic>P</italic> ≤ 0.016). <sentence_start/>Fentanyl also blunted the exercise-induced increase in mean arterial pressure, with a greater blood pressure-lowering effect of −10 to 13 mmHg observed in hypoxia (<italic>condition</italic>×<italic>P</italic><italic><sub>I</sub></italic><italic>O</italic><italic><sub>2</sub></italic>, <italic>P</italic> = 0.021). <sentence_start/>In contrast fentanyl increased circulating lactate and hydrogen ion concentration ([H<sup>+</sup>]) (<italic>P</italic> < 0.001), an effect accentuated during acute hypoxia (lactate: +1-2 mmol L<sup>−1</sup>, [H<sup>+</sup>]: +2-5 nmol L<sup>−1</sup>) but attenuated after acclimatisation (<italic>interactions</italic>, <italic>P</italic> ≤ 0.034). <sentence_start/>Thus group III/IV afferent feedback becomes more consequential in hypoxia, as small perturbations in ventilatory control and perfusion pressure have amplified consequences for oxygen transport.
Graphical Abstract

Participants completed cycling exercise with (placebo) and without (25 μg intrathecal fentanyl) intact group III/IV muscle afferent feedback in three settings: normoxia, acute hypoxia and chronic hypoxia after 7-9 days of acclimatisation (~3800 m). <sentence_start/>Blocking afferent feedback suppressed exercise hyperpnoea across all environments, but resulted in larger reductions in arterial oxygenation in hypoxia. <sentence_start/>Fentanyl also attenuated the exercise-induced increase in mean arterial pressure, with a greater blood pressure-lowering effect observed in hypoxia. <sentence_start/>In contrast circulating lactate and hydrogen ion concentration ([H<sup>+</sup>]) increased, particularly during acute hypoxia, with partial attenuation after acclimatisation. <sentence_start/>These findings demonstrate that group III/IV afferent feedback plays a critical role in maintaining arterial oxygenation and perfusion pressure during exercise, with heightened physiological importance in hypoxia where small disruptions to ventilatory control and cardiovascular regulation have amplified consequences for oxygen transport.
Introduction

Neural feedback from unmyelinated and thinly myelinated group III and IV muscle afferent fibres plays an essential role in regulating the ventilatory and cardiovascular responses to physical activity (<citation rid="R1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/japplphysiol.00462.2010" pmcid="PMC2963332" pmid="20634355" count="1">Amann et al., 2010</citation>; <citation rid="R43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1113/JP284870" pmcid="PMC10592099" pmid="37698303" count="1">Thurston et al., 2023</citation>). <sentence_start/>Specifically feedback from these group III/IV muscle afferents ensures normal exercise hyperpnoea (<citation rid="R1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/japplphysiol.00462.2010" pmcid="PMC2963332" pmid="20634355" count="1">Amann et al., 2010</citation>), pulmonary gas exchange (<citation rid="R24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1113/JP286993" pmcid="PMC11493515" pmid="39316014" count="1">Iannetta et al., 2024</citation>) and - via their role in the exercise pressor reflex - suitable arterial pressure (<citation rid="R43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1113/JP284870" pmcid="PMC10592099" pmid="37698303" count="1">Thurston et al., 2023</citation>). <sentence_start/>Collectively these responses ensure a matching of oxygen delivery to oxygen demand.

Exercise in hypoxia presents a considerable cardiorespiratory challenge, fundamentally caused by decreased oxygen availability when demand is high. <sentence_start/>Decreased inspired oxygen pressure (P<sub>I</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) requires exaggerated exercise hyperpnoea to defend alveolar oxygen pressure ( ), which can lead to exertional dyspnoea (<citation rid="R10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1042/cs0740531" pmid="3370920" count="1">Chronos et al., 1988</citation>). <sentence_start/>However even with this augmented ventilatory response, the hypoxia-induced reduction in constrains the alveolar-pulmonary capillary oxygen pressure gradient, resulting in a diffusion limitation at mild-to-moderate exercise intensities (<citation rid="R11" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/0034-5687(71)90065-x" pmid="5112830" count="1">Dempsey et al., 1971</citation>). <sentence_start/>Given group III/IV afferents have a dominant role in mediating appropriate exercise hyperpnoea, pulmonary gas exchange and exertional dyspnoea (<citation rid="R14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1164/rccm.201203-0404OC" pmid="22822019" count="1">Gagnon et al., 2012</citation>; <citation rid="R24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1113/JP286993" pmcid="PMC11493515" pmid="39316014" count="1">Iannetta et al., 2024</citation>), their function during exercise in hypoxia is critical for appropriate oxygen transport. <sentence_start/>The precision of ventilatory responses to exercise in hypoxia is particularly important given small decreases in arterial oxygen pressure have exaggerated effects on oxygen saturation due to the shape of the oxygen-haemoglobin disassociation curve and therefore total oxygen content .

There is evidence to suggest that group III/IV muscle afferents interact synergistically with carotid chemoreceptors under acute hypoxic conditions (<citation rid="R46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/japplphysiol.00449.2020" pmcid="PMC7654695" pmid="32816637" count="1">Wan et al., 2020a</citation>; <citation rid="R47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1113/JP279456" pmcid="PMC7720421" pmid="32170732" count="1">Wan et al., 2020b</citation>), potentially enhancing oxygen transport when availability is limited. <sentence_start/>Similar to carotid chemoreceptors group III/IV muscle afferents are sensitive to hypoxia, with increased discharge rates observed during hypoxaemic muscle perfusion in anaesthetised cats (<citation rid="R19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/jappl.1992.73.6.2524" pmid="1490966" count="1">Hill et al., 1992</citation>). <sentence_start/>However it is likely that this heightened discharge rate in hypoxia reflects increased intramuscular metabolic strain imposed by reduced muscle oxygen delivery, such that hypoxia itself contributes little to the activation of group III/IV muscle afferents (<citation rid="R3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1089/ham.2008.1105" pmid="19555297" count="1">Amann & Kayser, 2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>Acclimatisation to chronic hypoxia results in several coordinated adaptations that act to restore despite a persistent reduction in P<sub>I</sub>O<sub>2</sub>. <sentence_start/>This restoration occurs initially via rapid hyperventilation, which increases and (<citation rid="R13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/jappl.1971.31.4.586" pmid="5111007" count="1">Forster et al., 1971</citation>). <sentence_start/>With more prolonged exposure, oxygen is concentrated in the blood first via contraction of plasma volume (<citation rid="R37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/ajpheart.00394.2022" pmcid="PMC9678412" pmid="36269645" count="1">Roche et al., 2022</citation>), and thereafter via expansion of total red cell volume (<citation rid="R40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/japplphysiol.01121.2014" pmid="25749449" count="1">Siebenmann et al., 2015</citation>; <citation rid="R41" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1113/JP284578" pmid="38051656" count="1">Siebenmann et al., 2024</citation>; <citation rid="R42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/physrev.1953.33.1.13" pmid="13013831" count="1">Stickney & Van Liere, 1953</citation>). <sentence_start/>Although the restoration of does not appear to attenuate peripheral locomotor muscle fatigue during exercise in chronic hypoxia (<citation rid="R2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/japplphysiol.00606.2013" pmcid="PMC3763067" pmid="23813531" count="1">Amann et al., 2013</citation>), these adaptations may mitigate some of the muscle metabolic strain imposed by acute hypoxia (<citation rid="R6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-025-98762-x" pmcid="PMC12018925" pmid="40269052" count="1">Bejder et al., 2025</citation>; <citation rid="R20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/jappl.1992.73.2.728" pmid="1400003" count="1">Hogan et al., 1992</citation>), thereby altering the activation and, consequently, the contribution of group III/IV afferent feedback during exercise. <sentence_start/>Limited data in rats exposed to 45 days of 9.5% oxygen suggest that chronic hypoxia desensitises type III/IV afferents to fatiguing stimuli and lactic acid infusion (<citation rid="R12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1164/ajrccm.164.8.2010135" pmid="11704599" count="1">Dousset et al., 2001</citation>). <sentence_start/>However these data have been appropriately criticised as they do not take into account the observation that baseline group III/IV afferent discharge is already considerably elevated in hypoxia and the net discharge in response to activating stimuli is still larger in chronic hypoxia compared to rats in normoxia (<citation rid="R3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1089/ham.2008.1105" pmid="19555297" count="1">Amann & Kayser, 2009</citation>; <citation rid="R19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/jappl.1992.73.6.2524" pmid="1490966" count="1">Hill et al., 1992</citation>).

In a randomised, placebo-controlled design, we examined whether acute and chronic hypoxic exposures alter the functional contribution of group III/IV muscle afferents to ventilatory, pressor and metabolic responses during steady-state exercise, using intrathecal fentanyl to attenuate afferent feedback. <sentence_start/>Exercise was performed at matched absolute workloads within three experimental settings: (1) sea-level normoxia, (2) sea-level acute hypoxia and (3) high-altitude chronic hypoxia after 7-9 days of acclimatisation. <sentence_start/>Given that exercise in hypoxia occurs on the steep portion of the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve, we hypothesised that intrathecal fentanyl-induced suppression of exercise hyperpnoea would have disproportionately greater consequences for and . <sentence_start/>We further hypothesised that group III/IV afferent feedback would make a greater contribution to the maintenance of arterial pressure during exercise in hypoxia. <sentence_start/>Finally due to the heightened metabolic strain imposed by acute hypoxia, we hypothesised that suppression of group III/IV muscle afferent feedback would lead to greater increases in circulating lactate and hydrogen ion concentration in this setting than in normoxia and that this effect would be attenuated after acclimatisation, secondary to adaptations in .
Methods
Ethical approval

Ethical approval was granted by the University of British Columbia Research Ethics Board (H22-01091) and conformed to the <italic>Declaration of Helsinki</italic> (2013), with prior registration at (ID: ). <sentence_start/>Prior to participation, written informed consent was obtained from all participants.
Participants

Seventeen healthy participants (7 females) volunteered to take part in the study (age, 27.9 ± 5.3 years; body mass, 69.8 ± 9.6 kg; height, 173.5 ± 9.9 cm; maximal oxygen consumption , 50.8 ± 7.4 mL·min<sup>−1</sup>·kg<sup>−1</sup>). <sentence_start/>Participants were non-smokers, without cardiovascular or respiratory disease, and each refrained from vigorous exercise and alcohol consumption for 24 h before participation. <sentence_start/>The investigation consisted of sea-level and high-altitude visits; three participants (1 female) were unavailable for sea-level testing, whereas the remaining 14 participated in both environments.
Experimental design

The study utilised a repeated-measures doubled-blind cross-over design in which participants completed two identical cycling tests at sea level (Kelowna, BC, Canada: 340 m) and repeated them 3 months later, after 7-9 days of acclimatisation at high altitude (Barcroft Station, White Mountain, CA, USA: 3800 m). <sentence_start/>This timeframe was selected to coincide with substantial restoration of , consistent with evidence that the major haematological adaptations to altitude occur within ~2 weeks at comparable altitude (<citation rid="R34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/ajpregu.00725.2003" pmid="15191909" count="1">Lundby et al., 2004</citation>). <sentence_start/>Within each experimental visit participants were administered subcutaneous saline at L3-L5 (CON) or fentanyl intrathecally at L3-L5 (FENT) to isolate the role of locomotor group III/IV muscle afferents on exercise responses in hypoxia. <sentence_start/>Cycling conditions were separated by ≥3 days to limit potential carry-over effects, whereas time of day was matched within each participant (±1 h) to minimise diurnal effects.
Experimental protocol

During a preliminary lab visit participants completed a maximal incremental exercise test on a cycle ergometer (Kickr, Wahoo, Atlanta, GA, USA) to determine and establish constant load exercise intensities. <sentence_start/>tests were performed once each at sea level and high altitude, with the testing conducted at sea level used to determine the constant load work rates corresponding to 45%, 60% and 75% of normoxic . <sentence_start/>G was reduced by ~23% at high altitude, mean power outputs of 90, 135 and 185 W at sea level corresponded to ~60%, 75% and 90% of high-altitude .

On experimental trial days, following brachial artery cannulation, participants rested in a seated position for 8 min (resting baseline) and then completed 3 min of arm ergometry before and 2-3 min after intrathecal administration of fentanyl (FENT) or subcutaneous administration of normal saline (CON). <sentence_start/>A neuromuscular assessment was then conducted before participants were seated on a cycle ergometer. <sentence_start/>The exercise protocol began with 3 min of seated rest while breathing room air, followed by 3-min cycling bouts at 45%, 60% and 75% sea-level (mean external power: 90, 135, 185 W). <sentence_start/>Immediately upon completing the final bout, participants were switched to a Douglas bag delivering a hypoxic gas mixture ( , P<sub>I</sub>O<sub>2</sub> = 90 mmHg, equivalent to the P<sub>I</sub>O<sub>2</sub> expected at 3800 m). <sentence_start/>After a further 3 min of seated rest, participants repeated the 3-min exercise bouts at the same external work rates, that is, 90, 135 and 185 W, corresponding to a higher proportion of hypoxic . <sentence_start/>At high altitude the order of hypoxic exposure was preserved, meaning participants breathed first from a Douglas bag containing hyperoxic gas ( , P<sub>I</sub>O<sub>2</sub> = 139 mmHg) to mimic sea-level inspired oxygen, before switching to room air for the hypoxic bouts. <sentence_start/>It is important to note that seated ‘rest’ values were collected immediately before exercise began but after several preceding procedures (e.g. arm ergometry, neuromuscular assessments, intrathecal injection). <sentence_start/>As such, they likely reflect a mildly elevated physiological state and are best interpreted as ‘pre-exercise values’ rather than true resting values. <sentence_start/>This particularly applies to sea-level hypoxia and high-altitude hypoxic stages which follow the normoxic/hyperoxic exercise bouts. <sentence_start/>Blood samples and perceptual responses were obtained at the end of each exercise stage, while cardiorespiratory responses were recorded continuously (see Fig. 1).
Measurements
Blood sampling.

A local anaesthetic (1% lidocaine) was injected superficial to the brachial artery prior to cannulation. <sentence_start/>Using ultrasound guidance, the brachial artery was cannulated with a 20-gauge cannula (Arrow, Markham, ON, Canada), with the alternate arm cannulated during the subsequent condition. <sentence_start/>The cannula was connected in series to a wasteless sampling system (VAMP, Edwards Lifesciences, Irvine, CA, USA) and a pressure transducer, which was levelled to the height of the right atrium for continuous beat-by-beat intra-arterial blood pressure monitoring (ADInstruments, Dunedin, NZ) providing measurements of systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP) and mean arterial pressure (MAP). <sentence_start/>Blood samples were analysed immediately for pH, , bicarbonate concentration ([HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>]), hydrogen ion concentration ([H<sup>+</sup>]), haematocrit (Hct), haemoglobin concentration ([Hb]) and blood glucose and lactate concentrations using an ABL90 FLEX blood gas analyser (Radiometer, Copenhagen, Denmark). <sentence_start/>Rectal temperature was measured continuously using a T-type general-purpose sterile thermistor (ADInstruments) inserted ~15 cm beyond the sphincter. <sentence_start/>Arterial blood gas measurements were temperature corrected to the rectal temperature at the time of sampling using previously derived constants and logarithmic equations (<citation rid="R39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/jappl.1966.21.3.1108" pmid="5912737" count="1">Severinghaus, 1966</citation>).
Exercise responses.

Ventilation and pulmonary gas exchange were measured breath by breath at rest and throughout exercise stages via a metabolic cart (Vyntus CPX, Vyaire Medical, Mettawa, IL, USA). <sentence_start/>Heart rate (HR) was measured continuously (beat to beat) from the R-R period of ventricular depolarisation (H10, Polar, Kempele, Finland) and converted to digital signal for storage on computer software (SentrySuite, Vyaire Medical). <sentence_start/>Additionally in the final 15 s of each steady-state exercise stage, participants were asked to give subjective scores of dyspnoea and leg discomfort using Borg’s modified CR10 scale (<citation rid="R9" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Borg, 1998</citation>).
Intrathecal fentanyl.

Participants were seated in a flexed position, and 0.025 mg of fentanyl was administered intrathecally at the L3-L5 vertebral interspace, as has been detailed previously (<citation rid="R4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1113/jphysiol.2008.163303" pmcid="PMC2670040" pmid="19015193" count="1">Amann et al., 2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>Fentanyl remains active for ~60 min after administration and blocks ~50% of the feedback from the legs without impairing muscle strength (<citation rid="R1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/japplphysiol.00462.2010" pmcid="PMC2963332" pmid="20634355" count="1">Amann et al., 2010</citation>; <citation rid="R23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/japplphysiol.00490.2019" pmcid="PMC6879838" pmid="31513446" count="1">Hureau et al., 2019</citation>). <sentence_start/>To determine whether fentanyl migrated beyond the cervical spinal cord and influenced medullary <italic>μ</italic>-opioid receptors involved in breathing, we assessed ventilatory responses to a standardised arm-ergometry task (30 W for 3 min; Monark 881E, Monark Sports & Medical, Vansbro, Sweden) before and after drug administration. <sentence_start/>This evaluation was necessary, as cephalad migration of fentanyl into brain regions controlling respiration could complicate data interpretation (<citation rid="R29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.resp.2008.02.004" pmcid="PMC2642894" pmid="18394974" count="1">Lalley, 2008</citation>). <sentence_start/>Ventilatory responses to arm cycling before and after fentanyl administration were assessed on an individual basis. <sentence_start/>Reductions greater than 2 SD from the breath-by-breath recording of minute ventilation during the final minute of arm cycling observed in CON were considered evidence of a cephalic migration of fentanyl (<citation rid="R43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1113/JP284870" pmcid="PMC10592099" pmid="37698303" count="1">Thurston et al., 2023</citation>). <sentence_start/>HR and arterial blood pressure were also monitored during the arm-ergometry task; however due to the positioning of the arterial catheter and movement artefact associated with upper-body exercise, blood pressure signals were not considered sufficiently reliable for analysis. <sentence_start/>To ensure protocol consistency across testing days, the same arm-ergometry assessment was performed following saline administration.
Statistical analyses

Analyses were conducted in R (version 4.5.2, R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) using linear mixed-effects models, implemented using the lme4, lmerTest and emmeans packages. <sentence_start/>Condition (FENT, CON), P<sub>I</sub>O<sub>2</sub> (normoxia, hypoxia), acclimatisation (sea level, high altitude) and intensity (~90, ~135, ~185 W) were included as fixed effects, with participant modelled as a random factor. <sentence_start/>Rest data were not included in the statistical models and appear only in figures for contextual reference. <sentence_start/>Paired (within-subject) <italic>t</italic> tests were performed on seated rest data to confirm the absence of physiological effects of intrathecal fentanyl under resting conditions. <sentence_start/><italic>A priori</italic> planned contrasts tested the fentanyl-control delta for (1) acute hypoxia (sea-level hypoxia <italic>vs</italic>. sea-level normoxia, <italic>P</italic><italic><sub>I</sub></italic><italic>O</italic><italic><sub>2</sub></italic> effect) and (2) acclimatisation (high-altitude hypoxia <italic>vs</italic>. sea-level hypoxia, <italic>acclimatisation</italic> effect). <sentence_start/>Because neither <italic>condition</italic> × <italic>P</italic><italic><sub>I</sub></italic><italic>O</italic><italic><sub>2</sub></italic> × <italic>intensity</italic> nor <italic>condition</italic> × <italic>acclimatisation</italic> × <italic>intensity</italic> interactions were present, fentanyl-control effects are averaged across intensities. <sentence_start/>Main effects of intensity are reported separately. <sentence_start/><italic>P</italic>-values were calculated using the Satterthwaite method with <italic>α</italic> = 0.05. <sentence_start/>Results are presented as observed mean differences (Δ; fentanyl-control) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and units; data are mean ± SD unless stated otherwise. <sentence_start/>Figures and data were obtained using GraphPad Prism (version 10.6.1, GraphPad Software Inc., San Diego, CA, USA).
Results
Tests of cephalad drug migration

Each participant’s ventilatory response to arm cycling in FENT was within 2 SD of CON. <sentence_start/>The mean minute ventilation during arm cycling at 30 W (~41 ± 8 L·min<sup>−1</sup>) was not different between conditions (<italic>P</italic> = 0.111). <sentence_start/>HR during arm cycling (~123 ± 1.3 bpm) was also not different between CON and FENT (<italic>P</italic> = 0.148). <sentence_start/>These findings argue against a direct effect of fentanyl on cortical opioid receptors and are consistent with the absence of cephalad drug migration. <sentence_start/>For maximal voluntary contraction of the knee extensors, there was no difference between CON and FENT at sea level (<italic>P</italic> = 0.207) or high altitude (<italic>P</italic> = 0.509) prior to cycling, indicating that efferent nerve activity and quadriceps strength were unaffected by intrathecal fentanyl.

Additionally intrathecal fentanyl had no effect on any measured cardiorespiratory, metabolic or perceptual variables during seated resting conditions (i.e. prior to the onset of cycling exercise) at either sea level or high altitude. <sentence_start/>Unless otherwise stated all subsequent results refer to steady-state exercise responses.
Inspired oxygen partial pressure control

P<sub>I</sub>O<sub>2</sub> was reduced at sea level to simulate hypoxia equivalent to 3800 m altitude, allowing distinction between the effects of acute and chronic hypoxic exposure. <sentence_start/>Room air P<sub>I</sub>O<sub>2</sub> averaged 139 ± 1 mmHg at sea level and 91 ± 1 mmHg at high altitude, and was closely matched during gas administration (sea-level hypoxia: 90 ± 1 mmHg). <sentence_start/>Importantly P<sub>I</sub>O<sub>2</sub> did not differ between control and fentanyl conditions (<italic>P</italic> = 0.461; Table 1) at each altitude.
Ventilatory control during steady-state exercise
Exercise hyperpnoea.

When participants breathed room air at sea level, increased with exercise intensity (<italic>P</italic> < 0.001; Table 1; Fig. 2). <sentence_start/>Acute hypoxia further increased exercise hyperpnoea by an average of 18 L·min<sup>−1</sup> (<italic>P</italic> < 0.001; [15, 20]), and this was further increased by 11 L·min<sup>−1</sup> after acclimatisation (<italic>P</italic> < 0.001; [9, 14]). <sentence_start/>Increases in during acute hypoxia and after acclimatisation were mediated almost exclusively by increases in breathing frequency (Fb; Table 1). <sentence_start/>Intrathecal fentanyl suppressed exercise hyperpnoea in all environments by 3 L·min<sup>−1</sup> (<italic>P</italic> < 0.001; [−5, −2]), with no differential effects in acute hypoxia or after acclimatisation. <sentence_start/>Interestingly the effect of intrathecal fentanyl on suppressing Fb was greater after acclimatisation to high altitude (<italic>condition</italic> × <italic>acclimatisation</italic>, <italic>P</italic> = 0.008; Table 1).
Exercise hyperventilation.

During room air breathing at sea level, increased with exercise intensity (<italic>P</italic> < 0.001; Table 1; Fig. 3A). <sentence_start/>On the contrary, exercise in acute hypoxia caused to progressively decrease (Δ = −6 mmHg <italic>vs</italic>. normoxia, <italic>P</italic> <0.001; [−6.6, −5.4]), and this was even greater after acclimatisation (Δ = −8 mmHg <italic>vs</italic>. acute hypoxia, <italic>P</italic> < 0.001; [−8.8, −7.6]). <sentence_start/>Across all environments intrathecal fentanyl increased by 1.9 mmHg (<italic>P</italic> < 0.001; [1.5, 2.3]). <sentence_start/>Intrathecal fentanyl did not differentially affect in acute hypoxia or after acclimatisation (<italic>interactions, P</italic> ≥ 0.511). <sentence_start/>As expected, the ventilatory equivalent for CO<sub>2</sub> followed a similar pattern (Fig. 3B).
Pulmonary gas exchange and arterial oxygenation
Alveolar and arterial oxygen tension.

When participants breathed room air at sea level, increased with exercise intensity (<italic>P</italic> < 0.001; Table 1). <sentence_start/>Acute hypoxia substantially reduced (Δ = −34 mmHg <italic>vs</italic>. normoxia, <italic>P</italic> < 0.001; [−35, −33]). <sentence_start/>The decrease in was partially restored after acclimatization (Δ = 7 mmHg <italic>vs</italic>. acute hypoxia, <italic>P</italic> < 0.001; [5.9, 8.1]). <sentence_start/>Across all environments intrathecal fentanyl reduced by 1.6 mmHg (<italic>P</italic> < 0.001; [−2.3, −0.8]), with no differential effects in acute hypoxia or after acclimatisation (<italic>interactions</italic>, <italic>P</italic> ≥ 0.41).

When participants breathed room air at sea level, decreased with exercise intensity (<italic>P</italic> < 0.001; Table 1). <sentence_start/>As expected, acute hypoxia substantially reduced (Δ = −39 mmHg <italic>vs</italic>. normoxia, <italic>P</italic> < 0.001; [−41, −38]). <sentence_start/>The decrease in was partially restored after acclimatisation (Δ = 7.9 mmHg <italic>vs</italic>. acute hypoxia, <italic>P</italic> < 0.001; [6.6, 9.2]). <sentence_start/>Across all environments intrathecal fentanyl reduced by 2.5 mmHg (<italic>P</italic> < 0.001; [−3.4, −1.6]), with no differential effects in acute hypoxia or after acclimatisation (<italic>interactions</italic>, <italic>P</italic> ≥ 0.144).
Alveolar-arterial oxygen difference.

When participants breathed room air at sea level, higher exercise intensities increased the alveolar-arterial oxygen difference (A-aDO<sub>2</sub>; <italic>P</italic> < 0.001; Table 1; Fig. 4). <sentence_start/>The exercise-induced increase in A-aDO<sub>2</sub> was 5.9 mmHg greater in acute hypoxia (<italic>P</italic> < 0.001; [5.0, 6.8]) and remained similarly elevated with acclimatisation (<italic>P</italic> = 0.18 <italic>vs</italic>. acute hypoxia). <sentence_start/>Across all environments intrathecal fentanyl increased A-aDO<sub>2</sub> by 0.8 mmHg (<italic>P</italic> = 0.013; [0.2, 1.4]), with effects observed primarily at low exercise intensities. <sentence_start/>The effect of intrathecal fentanyl on A-aDO<sub>2</sub> was not different in acute hypoxia or after acclimatisation (<italic>interactions</italic>, <italic>P</italic> ≥ 0.186).
Arterial oxygenation and concentration.

When participants breathed room air at sea level, dyspnoea increased with exercise intensity (<italic>P</italic> < 0.001; Table 4). <sentence_start/>Acute hypoxia elevated dyspnoea by 66% (<italic>P</italic> < 0.001; [54, 77]), and this response was partially reduced after acclimatisation (Δ = −8%, <italic>P</italic> = 0.022; [−15, −1]). <sentence_start/>Across all environments intrathecal fentanyl lowered dyspnoea by 19% (<italic>P</italic> < 0.001; [−25, −12]). <sentence_start/>The effect of FENT on dyspnoea was not different in acute hypoxia (<italic>condition</italic> × <italic>P</italic><italic><sub>I</sub></italic><italic>O</italic><italic><sub>2</sub></italic>, <italic>P</italic> = 0.496) or after altitude acclimatisation (<italic>condition</italic> × <italic>acclimatisation</italic>, <italic>P</italic> = 0.299).

Discussion

This study examined how acute and chronic hypoxic exposures modify the functional contribution of group III/IV muscle afferent feedback to ventilatory, pressor and metabolic responses during steady-state exercise. <sentence_start/>The principal finding was that intrathecal fentanyl suppressed exercise hyperpnoea to a similar extent across environments, but this suppression resulted in larger reductions in and in hypoxia, consistent with operation on the steep portion of the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve. <sentence_start/>In parallel, group III/IV afferent feedback made a substantial contribution to the maintenance of arterial pressure during exercise, with a greater reliance on this reflex control in hypoxia. <sentence_start/>In contrast, the influence of group III/IV afferents on circulating lactate and [H<sup>+</sup>] was augmented specifically during acute hypoxia and attenuated following acclimatisation, consistent with a greater afferent contribution when muscle oxygen delivery is most constrained and a reduced contribution as is partially restored. <sentence_start/>Collectively these findings indicate that the functional importance of group III/IV muscle afferent feedback is heightened in hypoxia, not via disproportionate augmentation of ventilatory drive but through the amplified consequences of small perturbations in ventilatory control and perfusion pressure for oxygen transport when oxygen availability is limited.
Group III/IV afferents assume greater importance for arterial oxygenation during exercise in hypoxia

The equal suppression of exercise hyperpnoea by intrathecal fentanyl in normoxia, acute hypoxia and chronic hypoxia suggests that group III/IV afferents do not drive the pronounced hyperventilation observed in hypoxia. <sentence_start/>Our data therefore support the postulate that the carotid body is primarily responsible for both the acute hypoxic ventilatory response and the respiratory acclimatisation to hypoxia (<citation rid="R15" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1113/JP289355" pmid="41014645" count="1">Getu et al. 2025</citation>; <citation rid="R31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/ajpcell.00265.2015" pmid="26764048" count="1">López-Barneo et al., 2016</citation>; <citation rid="R32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1183/09031936.00056408" pmid="18978138" count="1">López-Barneo et al., 2008</citation>; <citation rid="R45" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/jappl.1987.63.6.2403" pmid="3436874" count="1">Vízek et al., 1987</citation>). <sentence_start/>However it should be noted that despite equal decreases in and in the fentanyl condition across environments, the decrease in was exaggerated in hypoxia due to positioning on the steep portion of the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve. <sentence_start/>Thus, although the relative contribution of group III/IV afferents to exercise hyperpnoea was unchanged across environments, the role of this afferent feedback in maintaining and becomes more critical in hypoxia, where equivalent ventilatory suppression leads to a disproportionate decrease in arterial oxygenation. <sentence_start/>In addition recent evidence has identified a role for group III/IV afferent feedback in supporting gas-exchange efficiency during exercise (<citation rid="R24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1113/JP286993" pmcid="PMC11493515" pmid="39316014" count="1">Iannetta et al., 2024</citation>). <sentence_start/>We observed a similar widening of the A-aDO<sub>2</sub> in our fentanyl condition; however this effect was small relative to the independent effects of exercise and hypoxia. <sentence_start/>Therefore the primary role of group III/IV afferent feedback in protecting arterial oxygenation during exercise appears to be through precise control of exercise hyperpnoea.
Afferent feedback plays an increasingly important role in maintaining arterial pressure during exercise in hypoxia

Across all environments intrathecal fentanyl elicited a clear decrease in MAP, reaffirming that group III/IV afferent feedback contributes to the maintenance of arterial blood pressure during exercise. <sentence_start/>Accordingly the reduction in MAP observed with fentanyl is best interpreted as the net haemodynamic consequence of attenuated afferent input, reflecting changes in vascular and central cardiovascular control rather than a direct effect of afferent feedback alone. <sentence_start/>This blood pressure-lowering response is consistent with evidence that group III/IV afferent feedback accounts for ~50% of the exercise-induced upward resetting of the baroreflex operating point for blood pressure (<citation rid="R22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1113/JP275465" pmcid="PMC5899981" pmid="29388218" count="1">Hureau et al., 2018</citation>). <sentence_start/>For MAP the effect of intrathecal fentanyl was greater in hypoxia, indicating that group III/IV afferent feedback has a larger contribution to exercising blood pressure in hypoxia. <sentence_start/>Within this context the greater reduction in MAP likely reflects an increased reliance on afferent-mediated sympathetic vasoconstrictor support to maintain peripheral vascular resistance when oxygen availability is reduced. <sentence_start/>This observation aligns with the work of <citation rid="R47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1113/JP279456" pmcid="PMC7720421" pmid="32170732" count="1">Wan et al. (2020b)</citation>, who showed that suppressing group III/IV afferent feedback during single-leg exercise in acute hypoxia had a greater blood pressure-lowering effect compared to normoxia. <sentence_start/>The synergistic interaction between the chemoreflex and group III/IV afferent muscle reflex on MAP might be expected to increase with chronic exposure since carotid chemoreceptors increase tonic activity (<citation rid="R15" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1113/JP289355" pmid="41014645" count="1">Getu et al., 2025</citation>) and sensitivity (<citation rid="R13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/jappl.1971.31.4.586" pmid="5111007" count="1">Forster et al., 1971</citation>) with prolonged exposure to hypoxia. <sentence_start/>However, the increased role of group III/IV afferents to exercising MAP was unchanged from acute to chronic exposure. <sentence_start/>In fact the exaggerated effect of fentanyl in reducing SBP in acute hypoxia is completely eliminated after chronic exposure (Table 2). <sentence_start/>One possible explanation for this pattern is the reduction in plasma volume that accompanies sustained high-altitude exposure (<citation rid="R37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/ajpheart.00394.2022" pmcid="PMC9678412" pmid="36269645" count="1">Roche et al., 2022</citation>; <citation rid="R38" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1113/JP280601" pmcid="PMC7894546" pmid="33124686" count="1">Schlittler et al., 2021</citation>). <sentence_start/>Such reductions in central blood volume could plausibly lower venous return and preload, thereby diminishing stroke volume and constraining pulse pressure. <sentence_start/>In this context the capacity for SBP to decrease further when afferent drive is withdrawn may be limited. <sentence_start/>Although the mechanisms underlying these differences cannot be resolved with the present data, the consistent blood pressure-lowering response in FENT underscores the role of muscle afferent feedback in supporting arterial pressure when oxygen tension is limited, and highlights the heightened reliance on this feedback during exercise in hypoxia.

Despite this amplified reduction in blood pressure in hypoxia, the influence of group III/IV afferent blockade on HR was modest and did not differ across environments. <sentence_start/>Due to the decrease in MAP, a compensatory baroreflex-mediated tachycardia might be expected; however HR was only slightly reduced, suggesting that the haemodynamic effects of afferent blockade were not primarily mediated via chronotropic mechanisms. <sentence_start/>Instead this dissociation between HR and MAP is consistent with a dominant reduction in peripheral vascular resistance, alongside competing influences of reduced sympathetic drive, and maintained central command on cardiac control. <sentence_start/>This contrasts with the findings of <citation rid="R47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1113/JP279456" pmcid="PMC7720421" pmid="32170732" count="1">Wan et al. (2020b)</citation>, who reported a hyper-additive HR response during combined activation of the exercise pressor reflex and hypoxia-induced chemoreflex, interpreted as centrally mediated sympathoexcitation. <sentence_start/>The absence of a comparable chronotropic interaction here likely reflects differences in experimental context; <citation rid="R47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1113/JP279456" pmcid="PMC7720421" pmid="32170732" count="1">Wan et al. (2020b)</citation> examined reflex co-activation during single-leg knee-extension exercise under severe hypoxaemia, which reflects a much smaller stimulus on the exercise pressor reflex and greater stimulation of the carotid chemoreflex. <sentence_start/>Therefore the present findings suggest that, under whole-body exercise conditions, afferent blockade primarily alters vascular rather than cardiac components of the pressor response, although the precise mechanisms cannot be resolved from the present data.
Reflex control of metabolic strain is more critical in acute hypoxia and adapts with prolonged hypoxic exposure

Acute hypoxia imposes a significant metabolic challenge to contracting muscle, constraining oxygen delivery and thereby increasing reliance on anaerobic metabolism (<citation rid="R27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1748-1716.1987.tb08213.x" pmid="3673605" count="1">Katz & Sahlin, 1987</citation>; <citation rid="R36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/ajpendo.2000.278.3.E522" pmid="10710508" count="1">Parolin et al., 2000</citation>). <sentence_start/>These findings are well established in both biopsy and P-31 magnetic resonance spectroscopy (<sup>31</sup>P-MRS) studies, which demonstrate greater phosphocreatine depletion, inorganic phosphate accumulation and intracellular acidosis when oxygen availability is limited (<citation rid="R6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-025-98762-x" pmcid="PMC12018925" pmid="40269052" count="1">Bejder et al., 2025</citation>; <citation rid="R18" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/jappl.1999.86.6.2013" pmid="10368368" count="1">Haseler et al., 1999</citation>; <citation rid="R21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/jappl.1999.86.4.1367" pmid="10194224" count="1">Hogan et al., 1999</citation>; <citation rid="R33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00018-009-0146-8" pmcid="PMC11115669" pmid="19756383" count="1">Lundby et al., 2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>In the present study this amplified muscle metabolic strain was reflected by higher circulating lactate during acute hypoxia. <sentence_start/>Intrathecal fentanyl further increased blood lactate and [H<sup>+</sup>] relative to control, and these effects were greater in acute hypoxia than in normoxia, indicating that group III/IV muscle afferents may have contributed more to regulating metabolic strain when oxygen delivery was reduced. <sentence_start/>Notably, [H<sup>+</sup>] was elevated across all settings, which may reflect fentanyl-induced suppression of ventilation and consequent reductions in CO<sub>2</sub> clearance (<citation rid="R28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/NEJM199105163242003" pmid="1902283" count="1">Krapf et al., 1991</citation>), whereas increases in lactate more closely tracked the degree of metabolic strain. <sentence_start/>Prolonged exposure to hypoxia elicits a host of adaptations that collectively improve oxygen transport and lessen the metabolic strain of hypoxic exercise. <sentence_start/>Increases in (<citation rid="R5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1600-0838.2008.00827.x" pmid="18665947" count="1">Bärtsch & Saltin, 2008</citation>; <citation rid="R41" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1113/JP284578" pmid="38051656" count="1">Siebenmann et al., 2024</citation>), together with improved acid-base regulation (<citation rid="R26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1113/jphysiol.2002.035899" pmcid="PMC2342856" pmid="12611920" count="1">Juel et al., 2003</citation>) and enhanced muscle buffering capacity (<citation rid="R35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1089/ham.2008.1009" pmid="19115916" count="1">Mizuno et al., 2008</citation>), enhance oxygen utilisation and help delay intramuscular acidosis during exercise (<citation rid="R7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/jappl.1989.67.4.1456" pmid="2793749" count="1">Bender et al., 1989</citation>). <sentence_start/>Relative to acute exposure, acclimatisation to hypoxia may reduce muscle lactate accumulation at a given workload by lowering glycolytic flux and enhancing oxidative phosphorylation (<citation rid="R17" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/jappl.1992.73.6.2701" pmid="1490988" count="1">Green et al., 1992</citation>), though this response is not consistently observed (<citation rid="R44" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1113/jphysiol.2008.160846" pmcid="PMC2673779" pmid="19139048" count="1">van Hall et al., 2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, in the present study acclimatisation partly restored sea-level and was accompanied by smaller increases in blood lactate and [H<sup>+</sup>] during matched-workload exercise in hypoxia. <sentence_start/>Given that group III/IV afferents are sensitive to intramuscular lactate concentrations and [H<sup>+</sup>] (<citation rid="R25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/jn.01067.2012" pmcid="PMC3652219" pmid="23427306" count="1">Jankowski et al., 2013</citation>; <citation rid="R30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/jn.01344.2007" pmcid="PMC6195653" pmid="18509077" count="1">Light et al., 2008</citation>), the smaller fentanyl-associated perturbations in blood lactate and [H<sup>+</sup>] after acclimatisation are consistent with a reduced metabolic stimulus for afferent activation when oxygen transport is reestablished.
Group III/IV afferents contribute to breathing pattern adaptation after acclimatisation without alleviating dyspnoea

At matched absolute workloads ratings of dyspnoea and leg discomfort were 60%-70% higher in acute hypoxia and did not improve with acclimatisation. <sentence_start/>These observations provide insight into the mechanisms underlying perceptual strain in hypoxia. <sentence_start/>Despite acclimatisation increasing exercising ventilation by 22%, achieved through greater breathing frequency and a tidal volume reduced to ~60% of normoxic values, ratings of dyspnoea remained unchanged between acute and chronic hypoxia. <sentence_start/>Given that large intrapleural pressure swings contribute to dyspnoeic sensations (<citation rid="R16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/thx.51.7.677" pmcid="PMC472488" pmid="8882072" count="1">Gorini et al., 1996</citation>), this rapid, shallow breathing pattern may act to minimise perceptual strain when the overall ventilatory demand is high. <sentence_start/>Notably, the influence of group III/IV afferent activity on breathing frequency, rather than tidal volume, was enhanced in acute hypoxia and further amplified after acclimatisation. <sentence_start/>These findings suggest that group III/IV afferent feedback contributes to the development of the rapid, shallow breathing pattern that is naturally adopted during exercise in hypoxia.
Methodological considerations

Several methodological factors should be acknowledged when interpreting these findings. <sentence_start/>Intrathecal fentanyl only partially blocks group III/IV afferent feedback; it has been estimated that ~50% of this feedback remains intact (<citation rid="R22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1113/JP275465" pmcid="PMC5899981" pmid="29388218" count="1">Hureau et al., 2018</citation>). <sentence_start/>As such, the contribution of these afferents to the cardiorespiratory and perceptual responses observed here is likely underestimated. <sentence_start/>Although a number of observations argue against cephalad migration of fentanyl (including the absence of resting ventilatory or cardiovascular effects, and the lack of suppression of or HR during the arm-crank control experiment), the approach used to exclude central effects was indirect. <sentence_start/>Arterial pressure measurements obtained during the arm-crank control condition were not interpretable due to movement artefact, preventing direct assessment of blood pressure regulation in this setting. <sentence_start/>Consequently subtle central cardiovascular influences during exercise cannot be definitively excluded. <sentence_start/>Beyond the pharmacological considerations associated with intrathecal fentanyl, sea-level and high-altitude trials were separated by ~3 months and conducted in a fixed order due to the logistical constraints of the high-altitude expedition. <sentence_start/>However, the primary comparisons (fentanyl <italic>vs</italic>. control) were performed within setting and were randomised and blinded, minimising the potential influence of these factors on the key outcomes. <sentence_start/>Additionally, the 7- to 9-day altitude acclimatisation period represents an early stage of adaptation; with longer residence, continued haematological (<citation rid="R5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1600-0838.2008.00827.x" pmid="18665947" count="1">Bärtsch & Saltin, 2008</citation>) and muscular adjustments (<citation rid="R35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1089/ham.2008.1009" pmid="19115916" count="1">Mizuno et al., 2008</citation>) could further refine afferent control. <sentence_start/>Although systemic markers such as blood lactate and pH provide a general index of muscle metabolic strain, they do not fully capture the intramuscular milieu that governs group III/IV afferent activation (<citation rid="R8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1113/JP272283" pmcid="PMC5023715" pmid="27241818" count="1">Blain et al., 2016</citation>). <sentence_start/>The absence of direct assessment of intramuscular metabolites therefore limits mechanistic interpretation of the afferent-mediated responses observed here. <sentence_start/>Finally, the absence of direct measures of leg blood flow or oxygen delivery represents an important limitation, particularly due to the altered haemodynamic environment of hypoxia. <sentence_start/>Without concurrent measures of local perfusion, it remains uncertain whether differences in oxygen delivery or metabolic stability primarily underlie the observed changes in afferent contribution.
Summary and conclusion

Group III/IV muscle afferent feedback plays a critical role in regulating ventilatory and pressor responses during steady-state exercise in normoxic and hypoxic settings. <sentence_start/>The importance of this feedback is accentuated in hypoxia, where small perturbations in ventilatory control and perfusion pressure have amplified consequences for oxygen transport when oxygen availability is limited. <sentence_start/>Accordingly, intrathecal fentanyl-induced suppression of exercise hyperpnoea resulted in larger reductions in arterial oxygen saturation and oxygen content, alongside a greater blood pressure-lowering response in hypoxia. <sentence_start/>In contrast, the contribution of group III/IV afferents to circulating lactate and hydrogen ion concentration was accentuated during acute hypoxia and attenuated after acclimatisation, indicating that muscle reflex control of metabolic strain diminishes as oxygen transport is partially restored. <sentence_start/>Together these findings identify group III/IV muscle afferent feedback as an adaptive control mechanism that is essential for maintaining arterial oxygenation and blood pressure during exercise in hypoxia.

Key points
Group III/IV muscle afferent feedback contributes to normal exercise hyperpnoea and blood pressure regulation; whether its functional contribution is altered by acute and chronic hypoxia is unknown.

In a double-blind, placebo-controlled cross-over design, 14 participants completed steady-state cycling with intact (placebo) or attenuated (intrathecal fentanyl) group III/IV afferent feedback in normoxia, acute hypoxia and after 7-9 days of acclimatisation at 3800 m.

Intrathecal fentanyl suppressed exercise hyperpnoea similarly across environments but caused exaggerated arterial oxygen desaturation during hypoxic exercise, reflecting operation on the steep portion of the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve.

The blood pressure-lowering effect of intrathecal fentanyl was greater during hypoxic exercise; effects on metabolic strain were greatest in acute hypoxia and largely normalised after acclimatisation.

These findings highlight the functional importance of group III/IV muscle afferent feedback during hypoxic exercise, where small perturbations in ventilatory and pressor control have amplified consequences for oxygen transport.
